articles.title: Clichés we use
articles.content: CONVERSATIONS about Pakistan easily and comfortably slide into clichés. The phrase ‘land of the pure’ is a personal favourite. Different generations — from boomers all the way down to the millennials — are perhaps equally familiar with ‘Pakistan at a crossroads’. Used as a headline or caption, it can be comfortably deployed to describe the state of affairs within, regardless of the context — be it the time of the Cold War, or the post 9/11 world, or from democratic interludes to hybrid times. The guilt is not just of Pakistanis but also the rest of the world which sees the country through a fog of clichés. Within this hard country, or the most dangerous country in the world, are the leafy streets of Islamabad, the port city of Karachi and Lahore with its Mughal past. Politics is military-dominated, and people have a penchant for strongmen in uniform, while political parties are family enterprises. KP is known as the province of the warrior-like Pathans, and Balochistan is tribal. Sindh is feudal territory where generations of peasants have worshipped Sufis and the Bhuttos. While the descriptions may vary a bit, they all portray societies frozen in time where little has changed, politically and socially. Agreed that many of these clichés are the result of foreign coverage of a country that has been, for various reasons, open to the storytelling by others. But at this point, it is hard to say if the storytelling by others has shaped our thinking and analysis or vice-versa. Whatever the case, clichés now shape so much of opinion that even society at large has been oblivious to the changes taking place under their very noses. For instance, it took 20 years of an insurgency in Balochistan for most people to realise that the sardars were no longer in charge in the province; the cliché has yet to be abandoned in discussions and by those who want to control politics. Indeed, clichés are used not just to describe but also to define how the country’s politics is run. The latter continues to be dominated by dynasties; people are uneducated and don’t know how to vote for the right people — which is why democracy doesn’t work. For they don’t vote for ‘good’ people but for those who can help them withgali, mohallay ki siyasat, or local issues. Or they voted for personalities and cult leaders. The cliché might alter a bit here and there but the inability of the people to make the right choice doesn’t. It’s enough to try the patience of a saint. Or many among our stability-seeking saints. But the politicians have their own set of clichés, convinced that only their capability can save the country — be it the ability to make a deal, a road (or rather, many roads), or end corruption. No one else is good enough. To their credit, none of them think they can aspire to learn the art a rival may have mastered. With their one skill, they can save Pakistan, much like the heroes of yesteryear who wore shorts over skinny pants and worked alone to save the Metropolis or Gotham. But this is an old cliché — before Hollywood discovered that they could all be made to fly together to confront the bad guys. Others, too, view them through clichés — cults, populists, experienced politicians, deal makers. And then the favourite is about how all of them were born in the same nursery (of the green and brown kind). Or as the latest version in Urdu goes, they passed through the same gate, the point being that none of them is authentic or genuine enough. Till, of course, they suffer at the same hands. The cycle repeats itself each time — with a new Pygmalion; a new flower seller. And then come the clichés about how to fix this country. These, too, have not changed. In one of the clichés, the problem is always the older, more established politician. And their removal is the answer. Minus one at times, minus everyone at others. It wasBhuttoback in the 1970s andNawaz Sharifin the 1990s. And these days, it seems it’sImran Khan. Another is to rid the country of ‘kruption’; so what if each such effort seems to have done little to stop the scourge, which is growing by leaps and bounds. It’s a cliché, not reality. But there is an even better one. The effort to ensure a better, truer democracy. And it is never the politicians who are interested in this cliché; others always have it on hand to help the people, and give them better leaders and a rosier future. Its name keeps changing but not the good intentions. Sometimes, it means partyless elections, sometimes empowered local governments, one unit ormore provinces. Call a rose by any other name and all that. It is so familiar and yet so different. For the dream hasn’t changed even though the times have. So it appears the old system needs more than a reset. It needs an overhaul so powers are devolved and people are helped at their doorstep. And this time around, we don’t just need random educated, middle class people in power, but those who can be compared to say Sadiq Khan in London or Zohran Mamdani in New York. There was a time when Mustafa Kamal was what the people of Karachi (and beyond) deserved as nazim but now the aspiration is not as local as it was then. Times have changed — or have they, in the land of the pure, also known as Cliché-stan?
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: The perpetual weak link
articles.content: IS India a weak link that worries the architects of the Shanghai club and the BRICS group? The question is as urgent today as it ever was, its importance underscored further by a potentially crucial BRICS summit that Prime Minister Narendra Modi hosts later this month. Several factors may be at play to determine if India is indeed a weak link for BRICS. Every country has its core interests and India’s foreign policy today seems to be based on two key factors, one being the calculation as to who or what can best help deliver the core interest of the ruling elite, namely the consolidation of a majoritarian state, the Hindu rashtra. It’s all too well known that the financial foundations of Hindutva lie in the West, a fact that became even more obvious with the recentvisit by the head of the RSS to the US and Canada. Russia and China have scant interest in the ruling party’s ideology as long as it does not disturb the political furniture the two groups have worked hard to set up. The West, too, couldn’t care less about the dominant worldview of a country as long as it is a trusted ally. A classic indication here is the silent acceptance ofIsrael’s genocide of Palestinians. When Western human rights groups mount pressure on India over its treatment of religious and ethnic minorities, it’s more of a leverage to extract political outcomes than a pursuit of moral tenets. A second factor in framing foreign policy is the interest of major business houses aligned with the Modi government. A typical episode showed India’s vulnerability in theAdani affairin the US. The political quid pro quo to get relief in the corruption case would be hard to assess, but it would be equally hard to ignore. In the middle of this equation, a nagging frustration stalks Narendra Modi’s battle to project himself to the world as a visionary from India, most recently in the image of Mahatma Gandhi and Gautam Buddha. Last week, Modi cast himself in the role of the two visionaries he cited to Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, telling the Russian leader to terminate thewar in Ukraineso that the world could live in peace and prosperity. Putin is always inclined to be patient with India given the importance he attaches to New Delhi’s membership of the Shanghai club and the BRICS orbit amid the groups’ sharpening battle with the US dollar and Donald Trump’s revulsion at a multipolar world, which much of Asia, Africa and Latin America seeks. A nagging frustration stalks Narendra Modi’s battle to project himself to the world as a visionary from India. Putin heard out Modi, eyes lowered and feet tapping in lieu of rudely looking at his wristwatch. Donald Trump, too,wants Russia to terminate the waras does Europe, preferably by weakening Moscow and, if possible, by delivering a strategic defeat. They pine for the elusive outcome without leaning on any moral principles, though. To them, as for much of the world, wars are politics by other means. What is less discussed in the Indian media is the fact that the war between Russia and Ukraine was set off by the US and its European satellites, which had ignored Putin’s red lines and sought to plant Nato’s battle formations right on Russia’s borders. The war became imminent when the West staged a colour revolution to oust a Russia-friendly government in Kiev and installed one that would eventually lead to Volodymyr Zelensky’s elevation as the West’s costly catspaw. Modi’s message of peace in elliptical geometry — “move from unending war to end of war” — did not go unnoticed by those who witnessedIndia’s bruising conflict with Pakistan in May last year. Initiated as revenge for an unconscionableterror attack on Hindu tourists in Pahalgam, the war was curiously suspended with Trump’s self-proclaimed intervention but not closed. War or no war, hostility to Pakistan remains a major input in the consolidation of Hindutva. In other words, the tensions with nuclear-armed Pakistan and India could go kinetic at the time of nuclear-armed India’s choosing, Buddha’s and Gandhi’s moral tenets notwithstanding. Both revered legends were the eminences grises in the Nehruvian concept of the modern welfare state he wanted India to become. And Nehru’s idealism flowed equally from his belief in the Soviet system of a command economy as the one best suited to alleviate mass poverty created and deepened by the colonial plunder of India. Mao’s China, too, was moving along the path Nehru extolled, except that Nehru placed his quest in the framework of democracy. A similar path was followed by Deng Xiaoping’s economic liberalisation and Xi Jinping’s market consolidation, with neither leader loosening the grip on the command economy. “Horse racing will continue, stocks will continue to be traded, and dancing will continue,” Deng prophesied with the return of Hong Kong to China in 1997. Nehru’s fear of untethered capitalism sprang from his astute assessment that a system instinctively rooted in private profit was unworthy of trust for the impoverished masses. How true his instinct was can be glimpsed from the 800 million Indians on the food dole despite four decades of a World Bank- and IMF-prescribed free-market system. Modi’s desperation to be deemed a worthy heir to his iconic compatriots relies on his near-total control of the media. The frustration with failing to fit into the oversized shoes of Jawaharlal Nehru as statesman and prime minister, respected and admired widely at home and abroad, however, is particularly galling. The self-advertised image as a culturally inclusive leader banks on the goodwill earned by India’s freedom heroes, none of whom came from the Hindutva fold. Modi’s dual personality charge is occasionally reflected in his angry frown at home together with a free flow of invectives hurled at opponents and the ready laughter and embraces abroad. China and Russia would not be too worried by Modi’s dual personalities. What might perhaps concern them more is Hindutva’s deeply fraught investment in the West. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: Better learning
articles.content: IN mainstream schools in Pakistan, challenges abound. From resource constraints to technological barriers, from limited professional development opportunities to high teacher turnover, the teaching and learning landscape has been contending with several issues. Perhaps the most urgent concern is the large classes that preclude getting to know students personally. The beauty of traditional teaching lay in the connection students had with their teachers. In developing societies like ours, this connection is critical to progress as the teacher’s influence extends beyond children to their families and the larger community. Teachers in developing societies are seen to be contributing to building communities through values, mentorship and personal oversight. If a student dropped out of school, the teacher would be seen visiting their home to convince the parents to send the child back. “Excellence is never an accident”, as Aristotle observed. Teachers who demonstrate excellence are usually the ones who are willing to innovate through challenges. Large classes and limited resources often make personalised attention difficult. In this context, the teacher’s capacity for differentiated instruction is curtailed. However, there are ways to navigate these difficulties without overburdening the teacher. The first one would be to work with infrastructure. Back in the 1960s when John Dewey rearranged the furniture in his classroom to create spaces for collaboration, a simple change led to fantastic results. Grouping or round tables where students could work together, discuss and be involved in a hands-on learning experience was the focus of Dewey’s role for the teacher. The furniture rearrangement was replicated in schools worldwide. His methods are equally relevant in Pakistan today where the demands of technology-mediated education make it necessary to rethink teaching. Newer methods imply letting go of old habits. Most teachers now recognise that students cannot be taught with traditional methods. Academic achievement rests on catering to the needs of individual students. Newer methods would imply letting go of old habits such as passive classes where students listen to the teacher who enjoys a great deal of talk time. Students like to speak, get involved in hands-on work, critique what is being taught and work together. Clearly, a lot has to change in our classroom environment. In Dewey’s approach, the onus is on educators to create an environment conducive to changing the culture of learning and to develop ways for students to have an immersive experience. Studying can become a goal to be chased with a passion, rather than remain a chore. When teachers allow students to present their own learning, projects or concepts, they provide an opportunity to showcase achievement and, as students lead the class, their peers learn from them. A student who may not understand a teacher’s method, may benefit from their peer’s presentation. Those who are quick learners get to teach, and this gives the teacher a window to assess and differentiate between strong learners and those who need additional help. Another fantastic concept that Dewey introduced was the morning meeting and the closing circle — both meant to give students an opportunity to talk as the teacher checks in and ensures that the day begins and ends on a positive note. This helps students’ level of responsiveness throughout the day. Teaching excellence can also show up in how teachers enable each student — how much encouragement they can provide, how much empathy they have for the student’s academic struggle, how much patience they exhibit with a student’s lack of behavioural regulation. Each of these areas can be a game changer for a teacher who has managed to make the students feel valued, connected to learning and motivated to improve. Teachers can devise their own techniques of differentiation in lessons. Some students learn through examples, many others learn through manipulatives and context clues or by teaching one another. Others learn through an inquiry-based approach where they are challenged with higher-order thinking questions. Most differentiation tools have one thing in common: they involve the students in engaging with content as best as possible. Student engagement with content is important for all subjects, but especially useful if we are to teach problem-solving skills, develop motivation and curiosity to learn independently. Excellence in education is not so much about learning content as responding to it, building on what is learnt and being able to teach it further. After all, the most successful teachers are not the ones who produce teachers, but just great learners. The writer is a teacher educator, author and a Fellow of the Higher Education Academy, UK. The views above are her own and do not reflect those of her employer.
articles.author: Neda Mulji

articles.title: Resource curse
articles.content: AFGHANISTAN is becoming a classic case of the resource curse. Riven with factional fighting and reliant on a conflict economy, the theories of the resource curse are highly applicable to Afghanistan, presenting a gloomy prognosis of its economic and political future. Despite the much-touted claims of $1 trillion in untapped mineral potential, Afghanistan has failed to realise that potential due to internecine conflict amongst various factions. On the one hand, there is a major division between the northern factions and the Interim Afghan Government, better known as the Afghan Taliban. On the other, there is an intense rivalry within the IAG between the Kandahari faction led by Mullah Hibatullah Akhundzada and the Haqqani faction based in Kabul. There are rich mineral deposits in the north and east of Afghanistan where Tajiks, Uzbeks and Hazaras mostly live. These groups resent any extraction of natural resources on their lands through IAG-sponsored projects. The case of the Aynak copper mine offers interesting insights into the non-viability of the project. Problems include increased cost due to underground versus open-pit mining, lack of water for on-site smelting, high logistics cost for transportation of minerals away from the site, high cost of local power generation, and contentious royalty issues. The security cost due to attacks on Chinese workers has also been a dampener for investors. Deep down, the issue of internal jousting for control and royalty between the Kandahari and Haqqani factions is a major obstacle. If a country lacks strong political institutions and a sound industrial base, and is not well integrated into the world economy, its susceptibility to the resource curse is a given. If Afghanistan starts mineral exports without functional banking and economic institutions, it runs the risk of contracting ‘Dutch disease’, in which inflation and the consequent high cost of imports nullify the export advantages, besides discouraging investments in non-resource sectors. Another downside of the resource economy is the risk of encouraging authoritarianism. Infighting prevents Afghanistan from realising its mineral potential. The worst impact of the resource curse is the prolongation of internal conflicts due to the ability of criminal gangs and militant factions to earn rents through resource exports and to use those for the continuance of conflict. There are terrorist groups in Afghanistan, such as IS-K, Al Qaeda, ETIM, IMU and TTP, that are part of the internal and external conflict dynamics of the country. If these terrorist entities are in an ‘entente cordiale’ with the IAG, then they are also likely to stake a claim to Afghanistan’s mineral resources and use the income to consolidate their hold over the illicit Afghan economy. The internal conflict mosaic of Afghanistan also makes the actualisation of mineral resources extremely difficult as involvement in the extraction business by foreign companies might attract international censure along the lines of UNSC Resolution 1173. The real fight over $1tr in mineral reserves is presently between the Kandahari and Haqqani factions of the IAG. Both are competing not only in a military capacity but also in resource mobilisation, as a result of which the mineral-rich provinces, largely inhabited by non-Pakhtun communities, bear the environmental, social and economic costs while deriving limited benefit from resource extraction. Major mineral resources are found in Hazarajat (Bamiyan, Daykundi — copper, coal), the north (Badakhshan — gems, lapis; Balkh/Sar-e Pol — gas, coal), and the east (Nangarhar, Logar — copper, gems, jade). Though political power lies with the Kandahari faction, it was the business-savvy Haqqani faction based in the east that, after 2021, controlled customs, ports and the passport directorate, through which a huge share of state revenue flows. The Kandahari faction is now pushing back against that control by moving Haqqani-aligned officials out of customs and ports, replacing them with its own loyalists to wrest control of the most lucrative revenue stream in the country. The tense stand-off between the two factions continues as Kandahar deploys troops in Badakhshan to assert the central government’s authority while the Haqqanis still manage to divert mining revenue away from mining sites in the east. As for the people, they lose either way. Mining under this system has promoted child labour, environmental destruction, and forced displacement of proximate communities. The extraction happens on their land, the profits leave the province, and neither faction is accountable to them. Poor governance, non-existent institutions, terrorism, and a conflict economy have ensured that Afghanistan’s mineral resources have become a resource curse for that country.
articles.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua

articles.title: Redrawing the map
articles.content: IT has been quite something to watch a whisper become, in a matter of weeks, the state’s new “number one priority”. The trigger was the interior minister’ssurprising admissionat the Pakistan Economic Summit in late July that the present system had “collapsed”, and that new provinces and administrative reform were therefore urgently needed. The political earthquake was immediate. For the PPP, alreadyfuming over the AJK election, it was an insult added to injury. The president’sabrupt departure for Londonhas since fed a good deal of speculation. Some believe that he went to press his allies in government to drop the idea altogether. Others have pointed out that his exit echoes another, years ago, when the PPP was being asked to make choices it considered political suicide. What can be said with certainty, however, is that an impasse has been reached. The president had met the interior minister in London. Their interaction was recorded and shown in the media. It does not seem to have gone fruitfully. On his return, the minister doubled down on the need for new administrative units. The PPP answered with aSindh Assembly resolution rejecting new provinces, and with speeches declaring “no compromise” on the province’s geographical unity. The Sindh Assembly resolution deserves much more attention than it received given the implications for the drive for more provinces. Under Article 239(4) of the Constitution, the limits of a province cannot be altered unless the amendment is first passed by that province’s own assembly by a two-thirds majority. Sindh seems to have made its position plain by, at least symbolically, vetoing the proposal before it arrived at its door. Before the country is dragged through another ugly crisis, those pushing for new provinces must explain how they intend to clear the bar set by the Constitution. They should also share what the new assemblies, secretariats and offices will cost, and where the money is to come from when citizens’ own pockets are already empty. There is no question that Pakistan needs better administrative management, but the stated end of restructuring — ie, better service delivery at the grassroots — is already provided for in Article 140A, and could be achieved far more cheaply by reviving, resourcing and actually holding elections for local governments. Here, the political parties also share blame. They have spent decades hollowing out the LG system and alienating the citizenry. Any party that is unwilling to empower even a district council should not be arguing that the province is the only unit that matters. Therefore, though the LG system remains a less politically toxic option, it will only be considered an option if the political parties themselves make a renewed commitment to it. This is something they, too, must understand.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Sugar trap
articles.content: ONCE again, the government is preparing to repeat an experiment that has cost consumers dearly. The sugar industry claims a surplus of 1.03m tonnes and wants immediate export permission. The government should resist until it has independently verified that figure. It cannot let the industry set both numbers and policy. There is good reason for scepticism. The Sugar Inquiry Commission documented export subsidies, alleged supply manipulation, underreporting and heavy windfall profits. The Competition Commission found evidence of price fixing among millers and later imposed penalties. Neither inquiry produced convictions or structural reforms, and the same mills accused of manipulation are setting the surplus number the government is being asked to accept. The latest episode is instructive. The government authorised roughly 750,000 tonnes of exports after declaring domestic supplies sufficient last year. Retail prices soon crossed Rs180 per kilo, and authorities had to arrange imports. The state pockets export earnings when supplies look plentiful, spending those on imports, and makes consumers absorb the cost when calculations are wrong. This cannot happen again. Officials must independently reconcile production, stocks, consumption, exports, next year’s expected output and grower payments at the mill level before authorising shipments. A mishandled surplus could depress cane prices and hurt farmers. An overstated one could trigger shortages, inflation and another costly round of imports. The government must guard against both, without letting the sugar lobby dictate outcomes. That requires a transparent, rules-based framework: export volumes tied to a well-defined domestic reserve, with automatic restrictions once supplies fall below that level or prices rise sharply. Stock data should be verified by an independent body, and reconciliation figures published before export permission is given. Such a system would cut political discretion and make manipulation harder to sustain. The recurring sugar crisis is a governance failure. Successive governments have bent to industry pressure instead of building rules that can withstand it. The government keeps subsidising millers only to spend scarce foreign exchange importing sugar months later, privatising the gains and socialising the losses. The question is not whether Pakistan can export another million tonnes of sugar. It is whether the state can prevent the same commodity from being exported cheaply today and imported expensively tomorrow.
articles.author: Editorial
